statement: Named, dated colonial/state "Protection" legislation gave government-appointed authorities extensive control over Aboriginal Australians' movement, residence, marriage, and child custody, with documented (if usually indirect rather than ceremony-specific) effects on ceremonial life: Victoria's Aboriginal Protection Act 1869 (the first comprehensive statutory control regime; amended 1886, forcing people of mixed descent off reserves including Coranderrk, prompting William Barak's 1886 walking-petition campaign to Melbourne); Western Australia's Aborigines Act 1905 (Chief Protector as legal guardian of every Aboriginal child under 16); New South Wales's Aborigines Protection Act 1909, amended 1915 (removed the requirement to prove neglect before child removal); the Commonwealth's Aboriginals Ordinance 1918 (NT). No primary-text search confirmed a specific statutory clause in any of these acts directly criminalizing ceremonies/corroborees by name — the suppression these acts document is indirect (confinement, permit systems, missionary co-location), not a direct ceremonial ban; do not assert a direct ban without primary-text confirmation. At Hermannsburg Mission specifically: Carl Strehlow (superintendent to 1922) did not interfere with ceremonies conducted away from the mission but campaigned to persuade converts to abandon their own ceremonial participation; his successor Pastor F.W. Albrecht, working with Aboriginal evangelist Moses Tjalkabota, led a dated 1928 event at Manangananga Cave in which sacred tjurunga were deliberately desacralized by public exposure to the uninitiated, women, and children — a specific, named act of religious-object destruction Carl Strehlow himself had refused to carry out.

sources.citation: "Tjurunga or Christ?" Sacred Imagery at Hermannsburg (Springer chapter / ResearchGate).
